scope: Reports of reward hacking in systems of LLM agents: reward, score or approval obtained without the intended work being done, with that gap measured.

scale.1: partly: stated without the detail needed to act on it
scale.NA: does not apply to the study

question: Could an agent that reads only the paper determine this, or would it have to guess? (after ODD+LLM, arXiv:2611.08932, with the reader an AI agent and the paper's text alone; linked repositories are not opened in this pass)

conventions.parts: An item with several parts is determined only when every part that applies is, and partly when some are.
conventions.silence: Where the text describes a mechanism and names no limit, rule or exception, none is assumed. Where a reproduction would have to pick a value that the text does not give, the item is not determined.

Every study: the label is not purely programmatic
Several agents, or a model that checks: more than one agent or a checking model
A tendency or knowledge of the hack was: a tendency or knowledge was introduced

items.text: The intended outcome: how it is decided that the task was really done, as computed.
items.why: Without it the gap between reward and real work cannot be computed.
items.case: In CATCH and in Hu et al. the label of a hack is exactly the disagreement between the rewarded check and this one.

items.text: The rewarded signal: the reward, score or approval the agents receive, as computed, with every term and weight.
items.from: new; Gorsane et al. for classical training
items.why: It is what the agents optimize or are told they are scored on.
items.case: The steganography repository computes the reward differently from the paper's formula (found when its code was run in this project).

items.text: The rule that labels an episode as a hack.
items.why: It decides which episodes count.

items.text: For a label given by a model or by people: the model and prompt or the annotation procedure, and its agreement with a reference.
items.applies_when: the label is not purely programmatic
items.why: A label from another judge is another measure.

items.text: What the reported rate counts and over what: unit, denominator, exclusions.
items.why: It is the number a reproduction is compared with.
items.case: Rollout Cards: changing only the reporting rule moved reported scores by up to 20.9 points.

items.text: The tasks or data: source, version, selection and splits.
items.why: Other tasks give another opportunity.
items.case: Huang et al.: spontaneous hacks in 30.5% of research-pipeline cells and 2.9% of task-specific cells.

items.text: What makes the hack possible, stated so that it can be rebuilt.
items.why: Without the loophole there is nothing to exploit.

items.text: What an agent can read, write and run: files, tools, permissions, network.
items.why: A hack needs the means to carry it out.
items.case: Thaman: "Simple environmental hardening reduces exploit rates by 5.7 percentage points (87.7% relative)".

items.text: How to recreate the environment: image or commit, and dependencies.
items.why: Needed when the loophole depends on how one version of a tool behaves, such as a proof checker or a test runner.
items.case: Gorsane et al.: the version of the environment changed the ranking of algorithms.

items.text: What the agents see of the evaluation: tests, scores, feedback between attempts.
items.why: What an agent sees of the check shapes whether it games it.
items.case: Shi et al.: for one model "removing verdict review eliminates collusion entirely".

items.text: How hard the intended work is for these agents: whether it can be done at all within the limits, how often the same agents complete it without the hack or how the required score compares with the best result reached honestly, and whether an agent can decline or report that it cannot be done.
items.from: new; found by mapping what the collected studies varied or named as a driver (corpus.json, varied)
items.why: A hack is taken up when the honest route fails or pays less. With another checkpoint the same tasks are easier or harder, so the task list alone does not fix this.
items.case: Thaman: "Models with near-zero exploit rates on standard tasks show elevated rates on harder variants"; CATCH: "Making the reward harder to obtain accelerates reward hacking"; Huang et al.: two candidate tasks whose thresholds "were set in the wrong measured space" "produced no reward hack".

items.text: What the agents are told about being tested, watched or trained.
items.from: PIMMUR (unawareness) as a principle; found by mapping what the collected studies varied (corpus.json, varied)
items.why: What an agent takes the setting to be is a condition of what it does there, and the prompts set it.
items.case: Xiao and Phuong: a model trained "only on training awareness documents" developed "its own compliance gap" under reinforcement learning.

items.text: Each model by exact name and version or date, for every role.
items.why: The same setup gives other behavior with another checkpoint.
items.case: Naming game in this project: present with one checkpoint, absent with a larger one.

items.text: Sampling settings and limits: temperature, output and context limits, reasoning setting.
items.why: Temperature and limits change what is written and whether an episode completes.
items.case: Emergent Collusion code in this project: an output limit of 8,192 against the paper's 64,000 and a context of 262,144 tokens; steganography: unpadded prompts give another code.

items.text: System and task prompts verbatim, including whatever they say about cheating.
items.why: One sentence of a prompt has decided the behavior.
items.case: ODD+LLM, naming game: convergence 0.350 with the baseline wording and 1.000 with a first-person framing; PIMMUR: removing a steering instruction removed reported effects; this project: the sentence that asks for step-by-step reasoning.

items.text: The agent framework with version, its tools, stop rule, handling of history, and what happens after an invalid output: retries and the default action.
items.from: ODD+LLM DF-1, DB-4; disclosure schema (harness); ODD+LLM (retry policy, failure action)
items.why: What is kept in the history is the agent's memory.
items.case: Shi et al.: "removing cross-episode memory almost completely eliminates collusion"; Emergent Collusion code in this project: a reply with 524 calls of one tool was executed in full, the next request exceeded the context and the trajectory ended.

items.text: The number of agents, the role of each, and which are models and which are scripted or fixed.
items.applies_when: more than one agent or a checking model
items.why: The behavior is defined over these agents.
items.case: Shi et al.: "Replacing a compliant scripted peer with a violating one raises Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite’s ACCEPT rate from 13.6% to 41.2%."

items.text: Who can pass what to whom, and how much: messages, code, memory, plans, shared stores, any limit on them, and who sees them.
items.applies_when: more than one agent or a checking model
items.why: A hack spreads only along what is shared.
items.case: Paglieri et al.: the exploit spread through the shared library; Hu et al.: through code, memory and plans; Shi et al.: under a limit on the messages "the only compliant verdict is REJECT", and with unconstrained communication an agent can follow the protocol.

items.text: The order of turns and the number of rounds or episodes.
items.applies_when: more than one agent or a checking model
items.why: Order decides who sees what before acting, and a behavior can take many rounds to appear.
items.case: Shi et al.: agents "increasingly deviate from the protocol over repeated interactions".

items.text: Who checks whose work, what the checker sees and how its decision returns to the agents.
items.why: The checker is part of what is gamed.
items.case: Hu et al.: showing the evaluator's pass signal raised the verifiers' false accepts.

items.text: How reward or credit is divided among the agents and what competition exists.
items.why: Competition or a shared reward is the incentive.
items.case: Paglieri et al.: credit to the first solver and a lock on solved problems preceded the cheating.

items.text: What the agents were told or shown about hacking, so that the case can be labeled instructed, cued, seeded, spontaneous or trained, and whether a stated rule against it is enforced.
items.from: new; PIMMUR (minimal control) as a principle
items.why: It decides whether the behavior was asked for.
items.case: Hu et al.: "Prohibitions delay and reduce reward hacking but do not prevent it"; Bondarenko et al.: language models "need to be told that normal play won't work to hack"; Paglieri et al.: the rule "was not actively enforced beyond the autograder check".

items.text: How an initial tendency or knowledge of the hack was introduced: examples, documents or prompt, with amounts.
items.applies_when: a tendency or knowledge was introduced
items.why: A seeded tendency is an ingredient.
items.case: CATCH: hacking stays near zero at 4.5% hacking demonstrations and is sustained at 9.1%.

items.text: The training algorithm and which agents it updates: which are trained and which are frozen, whether they share weights, and the order of their updates.
items.why: Another algorithm is another training, and a behavior between agents depends on which of them learn.
items.case: Steganographic collusion in this project: task success 0.998 with sender and receiver trained and 0.553 with the sender's weights frozen and the receiver still trained; Zhou et al.: exploits "in several cases remain more persistent when learned through RL than when distilled through SFT".

items.text: The training configuration: learning rate, batch, rollouts, adapter settings, or the configuration file.
items.why: The configuration is the training.
items.case: The steganography repository's batch sizes and KL settings differ from the paper's table.

items.text: How long training ran, what ended it and how the reported checkpoint was chosen.
items.why: A behavior can appear only late in training.
items.case: Steganography in this project: absent after 100 cycles, present after 200; the paper says "until convergence".

items.text: The base checkpoint and the training data or mixture of environments.
items.why: The starting point and the data decide what can be learned.
items.case: Countdown-Code: about 1% of hacking traces in the fine-tuning data is enough.

items.text: Hardware and time.
items.why: It says whether one can afford the run. The settings that hardware constrains, such as a batch size, are items of their own.

items.text: The training library and its version.
items.why: Needed when the report leaves settings to a library's defaults.
items.case: Mathew et al.: "All our PPO hyperparameters are equivalent to the default values in the TRL library, unless otherwise stated", with no version.

items.text: Independent runs or seeds per condition.
items.why: It tells how far a single reproduction may differ by chance.
items.case: Mathew et al.: one of the seeds did not converge on the second dataset.

items.text: How run-to-run variation is reported.
items.from: ODD+LLM E3b, E4; Gorsane et al.
items.why: The same.

items.text: A condition that removes the claimed ingredient: the loophole, the sharing, the training or the seeded agent.
items.why: It is the result that shows which ingredient the behavior needs; without it only the presence of the behavior can be matched.

items.text: Failed, excluded or dropped runs, with counts.
items.why: Dropped runs change the reported rate.
items.case: Rollout Cards: none of 50 repositories reports failed or skipped runs beside its score.

items.text: Code at a stated address and version.
items.why: Not needed when the text settles the items above. It can settle many of them at once, and it is the only complete description when text and code differ.
items.case: Steganography: reward, batch sizes and the format of the sender's input are right only in the code.

items.text: Tasks or data at a stated address.
items.why: Needed when the tasks cannot be regenerated from their description, such as a selection or a generated dataset.

items.text: Transcripts or rollouts of the runs.
items.why: Lets a reader check that a reproduced behavior is the same in kind.

items.text: Trained weights or adapters.
items.why: Lets others study the behavior without repeating the training.

items.text: Tokens or money spent.
items.why: Planning.

needs.produce: needed to produce the behavior: left open, an agent has to guess a condition of the behavior
needs.judge: needed to judge a reproduction: left open, one cannot tell whether the same behavior was obtained
needs.conditional: needed only under the stated circumstance
needs.aid: not needed: it makes a reproduction cheaper, checkable or plannable

changes: 0.1: every item is marked by what it is needed for, after the maintainer's objection that materials, hardware, time and cost are not requirements; the training library and its version (E8) is split from the algorithm (E3).

0.2: B6 added (how hard the intended work is for the agents). Mapping what the 28 kept studies varied or named as a driver onto the items of 0.1 left 15 of 83 entries without an item; 13 of them, from 13 studies, are about this.

0.3: B7 added (what the agents are told about being tested, watched or trained); it is an item of its own because inside B5 a report that describes the feedback in full and is silent on this would lose B5's score over another fact. Wording extended in C4 (invalid outputs), D1 (scripted or fixed agents), D2 (limits), D3 (number of rounds or episodes), E1 (whether a stated rule is enforced) and E3 (which agents are trained). Cases added to B1, B3, B5, C4, D1, D2, D3, E1 and E3 from text checked on 2026-11-25. Two conventions of scoring written down. The seven audited papers were checked again on the changed items. The list is held at this version for the second scoring pass.
